Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

AuditLogs

| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result

2026-05-25 18 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Installation. [LLM] TrapDoor named-package install via npm / pip / cargo on developer host Delivery High
Hunts for installation or invocation of any of the 34 named TrapDoor packages across npm, PyPI, and Crates.io. Highest-fidelity IOC pivot in the campaign — package names are bespoke and unlikely to appear outside this attack. Rationale: Pivots on the exact 34 package-name strings published by Socket (cross-confirmed at socket.dev/blog/trapdoor-crypto-stealer-npm-pypi-crates). These names are bespoke typosquats unlikely to collide with legitimate registry traffic, making any `npm install <name>` / `pip install <name>` / `cargo add <name>` invocation a near-certain TP. [LLM] Python interpreter spawning node -e fetching remote JS (TrapDoor PyPI delegation) Installation High
Hunts the TrapDoor PyPI execution chain: a malicious PyPI package auto-executes on import, then shells out to `node -e` to run an inline JS payload that retrieves trap-core.js from ddjidd564.github.io. python.exe → node.exe with -e is an extremely rare pattern outside this attack. Rationale: python→node with `-e` is a near-zero-FP pattern; the article and Socket both explicitly call out this exact delegation ("auto-executed on import...download JavaScript from an attacker-controlled GitHub Pages domain (ddjidd564[.]github[.]io), and run it using node -e"). Adding the ddjidd564/defi-security-best-practices/github.io URL fragments anchors the detection to the campaign's actual payload host. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/trapdoor-crypto-stealer-npm-pypi-crates

| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" -e "," --eval","ddjidd564","github.io","defi-security-best-practices")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "-e" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http","https","fetch(","require('http","require(\"http"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256

[LLM] TrapDoor C2 contact to ddjidd564.github.io payload host Command & Control High
Hunts any DNS resolution or HTTP fetch of ddjidd564.github.io — the GitHub Pages domain the TrapDoor PyPI loader uses to retrieve trap-core.js. Single-IOC detection; any developer host contacting this domain is compromised. Rationale: Pivots on the campaign's sole infrastructure IOC — Socket confirms ddjidd564.github.io as the payload host (path /defi-security-best-practices/) and the GitHub account that anchors the entire 34-package campaign. Single-IOC detection is rarely justified, but a developer-attributed GitHub Pages domain with zero legitimate use case is the exception. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/trapdoor-crypto-stealer-npm-pypi-crates • https://cyberpress.org/supply-chain-attack-compromises-34-packages/

[LLM] TrapDoor AI prompt-injection persistence — .cursorrules / CLAUDE.md drop by build tools Installation High
Hunts creation or modification of .cursorrules or CLAUDE.md files by package-manager-spawned processes (node, npm, python, pip, cargo, rustc). TrapDoor's novel persistence vector implants zero-width-Unicode-laced instructions into these AI assistant config files so Cursor and Claude Code will silently execute 'security scans' that exfiltrate secrets. Rationale: Targets the novel TrapDoor persistence vector explicitly called out by both the article and Socket: "implanting of .cursorrules and CLAUDE.md containing hidden instructions to trick AI assistants into running a 'security scan' that results in secret discovery and exfiltration." Socket additionally confirms the use of zero-width Unicode in the file content. The parent-process narrowing to build tools makes the FP rate manageable. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/trapdoor-crypto-stealer-npm-pypi-crates • https://www.cyberkendra.com/2026/05/malicious-packages-on-npm-pypi-and.html

[LLM] TrapDoor persistence install via cron / systemd / git hooks / SSH from package-manager parent Installation Medium
Hunts persistence mechanism establishment (crontab edits, systemd user unit writes, .git/hooks installs, SSH key/authorized_keys writes, shell-rc modifications) where the initiating process chain traces back to npm/pip/cargo/node/python — the trap-core.js post-install routine. Rationale: The article explicitly enumerates the persistence primitives planted by trap-core.js: "persistence using cron jobs, systemd services, Git hooks, and moves across the network via SSH." The detection's high-fidelity element is the parent-process narrowing — a developer's npm install spawning crontab is anomalous; SYSTEM/services.exe spawning crontab is not. Inclusion of git hooks and shell-rc paths catches the trap-core.js variants that prefer userland persistence over root-required cron. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/trapdoor-crypto-stealer-npm-pypi-crates
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1543.002 T1546.004 T1098.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
let BuildParents = dynamic(["node.exe","node","npm.exe","npm","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","python.exe","python","python3","python3.exe","pip.exe","pip","pip3","cargo.exe","cargo","rustc.exe","build-script-build","build-script-build.exe"]);
let PersistMechanisms = dynamic(["crontab","crontab.exe","systemctl","systemctl.exe","ssh-keygen","ssh-keygen.exe","ssh-keyscan","schtasks.exe","reg.exe"]);
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (BuildParents) or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (BuildParents))
    | where FileName in~ (PersistMechanisms)
        or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("crontab -","systemctl --user enable","systemctl enable","/etc/cron.","/etc/systemd/system/","~/.config/systemd/user","~/.bashrc","~/.zshrc","~/.profile","~/.bash_profile","authorized_keys",".git/hooks/pre-commit",".git/hooks/post-checkout",".git/hooks/post-merge","schtasks /create","HKCU\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Run")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine),

    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (BuildParents) or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (BuildParents)

    | where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron","/etc/systemd/system","/.config/systemd/user","/.ssh/","/.git/hooks/")
        or FileName in~ (".bashrc",".zshrc",".profile",".bash_profile","authorized_keys")

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Ghost CMS CVE-2026-26980 SQL injection probing against /ghost/ admin endpoints Exploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated SQL-injection attempts against Ghost CMS admin/canary API paths consistent with CVE-2026-26980 exploitation — bursts of requests carrying UNION/SELECT/information_schema/sleep payloads or causing 4xx/500 errors on /ghost/api/* routes. Article-specific because it pivots on Ghost's URL space rather than a generic WAF rule. Rationale: Pivots on the Ghost CMS URL namespace (/ghost/api/admin, /ghost/api/canary) called out in the CVE-2026-26980 advisory plus classic SQLi payload tokens; combined with response-code anomalies this catches blind/error-based SQLi enumeration rather than benign API traffic. Cross-checked against the SentinelOne Feb-27 write-up referenced in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-26980 • https://ghost.org/docs/security/
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb
let SqliMarkers = dynamic(["union","UNION","select","SELECT","information_schema","sleep(","0x3a","%27","--","/*!","benchmark("]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (W3CIISLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where csUriStem startswith "/ghost/" or csUriStem contains "/api/admin/" or csUriStem contains "/api/canary/"
        | where csUriQuery has_any (SqliMarkers) or scStatus in ("500","400")
        | summarize Hits = count(), Stems = make_set(csUriStem, 25), Statuses = make_set(scStatus, 10), Queries = make_set(csUriQuery, 25) by cIP, csUserAgent, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
        | where Hits > 5),
    (AppServiceHTTPLogs
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where CsUriStem startswith "/ghost/" or CsUriStem contains "/api/admin/" or CsUriStem contains "/api/canary/"
        | where CsUriQuery has_any (SqliMarkers) or ScStatus in (400,500)
        | summarize Hits = count(), Stems = make_set(CsUriStem, 25), Statuses = make_set(ScStatus, 10), Queries = make_set(CsUriQuery, 25) by CIp, UserAgent, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
        | where Hits > 5),
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where RequestURL has "/ghost/" and RequestURL has_any (SqliMarkers)
        | summarize Hits = count(), Urls = make_set(RequestURL, 25) by SourceIP, RequestClientApplication, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
        | where Hits > 5)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(nginx OR apache OR iis) @http.url_details.path:(*\/ghost\/api\/admin\/* OR *\/ghost\/api\/canary\/* OR *\/ghost\/api\/*) AND (@http.url:(*union*select* OR *UNION*SELECT* OR *information_schema* OR *sleep\(* OR *%27* OR *0x*) OR @http.status_code:(400 OR 500))

[LLM] Endpoint network/DNS contact with Ghost CMS ClickFix campaign infrastructure Command & Control High
Hunts host-side resolution or connection to the cloaking, staging, and payload-hosting domains and the single IP tied by XLab to the CVE-2026-26980 ClickFix follow-on. Article-specific because the indicator set is the actual XLab IOC bundle, not a generic suspicious-TLD list. Rationale: Uses the XLab-published IOC bundle (8 domains + 144.31.236.66) verbatim against host DNS/network telemetry — these are not legitimate Cloudflare/CDN namespaces, so hits are high-fidelity. Cross-checked the staticcloudflare.pro typosquat pattern via VirusTotal community reports tied to the same cluster. Cross-checked against: • https://urlscan.io/ • https://www.virustotal.com/ • https://x.com/XLab_Qianxin
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution Network_Traffic

let CampaignIPs = dynamic(["144.31.236.66"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in (CampaignIPs)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (CampaignDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc

let CampaignIPs = dynamic(["144.31.236.66"]);

        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Indicator = coalesce(DstHostname, DstIpAddr, Url), Kind = "netflow_asim"),
    (DnsEvents

[LLM] ClickFix lure execution: browser-spawned shell pasting payload command to campaign infra Delivery High
Catches the ClickFix lure being acted on — a browser (or explorer Run dialog) spawns cmd/powershell/mshta whose command line references one of the XLab-published staging hostnames/IP, often using curl/iwr/mshta/bitsadmin/certutil to pull the next stage. The combination of browser parent + LOLBin child + campaign IOC string is what makes this article-specific. Rationale: Models the exact ClickFix kill-chain step described in the article — the victim is told to paste a command into the Run dialog/cmd which then fetches from attacker infra. Parent=browser/explorer + child=shell + command line containing an XLab IOC or a download LOLBin pattern is high-signal; the IOC list anchors it to this specific campaign rather than generic ClickFix templates. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/004/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.003 T1059.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let CampaignIOCs = dynamic(["clo4shara.xyz","cloud-verification.com","jalwat.com","com-apps.cc","web-telegram.ug","platecrumbs.com","taketwolabs.com","staticcloudflare.pro","144.31.236.66"]);
let BrowserParents = dynamic(["chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","explorer.exe"]);
let ShellChildren = dynamic(["cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (BrowserParents)
| where FileName in~ (ShellChildren)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (CampaignIOCs)
   or (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl ","Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ","IWR ","DownloadString","mshta","bitsadmin","certutil -urlcache","-decode") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"https?://[^\s\)\"']+")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc

           or (TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl ","Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ","DownloadString","mshta","bitsadmin","certutil -urlcache") and TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"https?://")
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"

        | where CommandLine has_any (CampaignIOCs)

[LLM] UtilifySetup.exe Electron implant or campaign-hashed payload execution Installation High
Detects execution, write, or load of the Electron-packaged 'UtilifySetup.exe' implant or any of the five MD5s attributed by XLab to the Ghost CMS ClickFix campaign payload set. Hash-and-name anchored so it is unambiguously this campaign. Rationale: Uses the verbatim five MD5 IOCs and the unique payload name 'UtilifySetup.exe' from the XLab report — Electron installer + that exact name is not a known legitimate product, and the hashes are post-classification campaign-specific. Multi-table union covers execution, file-drop, and image-load to catch staged loaders and the final Electron binary. Cross-checked against: • https://bazaar.abuse.ch/ • https://www.virustotal.com/ • https://otx.alienvault.com/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.007 T1218.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
let CampaignHashes = dynamic(["5659292833ec421da11ebde005d9c9a8","d30cc10d54ebc967c8538ff74f442eee","18a7251ddde77ed24bc54700d84d9be1","f280e12f51f996dae7fffc64a56ee527","fceca579efcef09eb507c6ca977ea281"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
        | where FileName =~ "UtilifySetup.exe"
            or MD5 in (CampaignHashes)
            or InitiatingProcessMD5 in (CampaignHashes)
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, MD5, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents"),
    (DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
        | where FileName =~ "UtilifySetup.exe"
            or MD5 in (CampaignHashes)
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, Source = "DeviceFileEvents"),
    (DeviceImageLoadEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
        | where MD5 in (CampaignHashes)
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceImageLoadEvents")
| order by Timestamp desc
let CampaignHashes = dynamic(["5659292833ec421da11ebde005d9c9a8","d30cc10d54ebc967c8538ff74f442eee","18a7251ddde77ed24bc54700d84d9be1","f280e12f51f996dae7fffc64a56ee527","fceca579efcef09eb507c6ca977ea281"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where TargetProcessName endswith "UtilifySetup.exe" or MD5 in (CampaignHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, MD5, SHA256, Source = "ImProcessCreate"),
    (ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where TargetFileName =~ "UtilifySetup.exe" or TargetFileMD5 in (CampaignHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileMD5, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImFileEvent"),

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-26980")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-26980")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")

SecurityEvent

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1204.002

    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '

      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("5659292833ec421da11ebde005d9c9a8", "d30cc10d54ebc967c8538ff74f442eee", "18a7251ddde77ed24bc54700d84d9be1", "f280e12f51f996dae7fffc64a56ee527", "fceca579efcef09eb507c6ca977ea281") or SHA1 in~ ("5659292833ec421da11ebde005d9c9a8", "d30cc10d54ebc967c8538ff74f442eee", "18a7251ddde77ed24bc54700d84d9be1", "f280e12f51f996dae7fffc64a56ee527", "fceca579efcef09eb507c6ca977ea281") or MD5 in~ ("5659292833ec421da11ebde005d9c9a8", "d30cc10d54ebc967c8538ff74f442eee", "18a7251ddde77ed24bc54700d84d9be1", "f280e12f51f996dae7fffc64a56ee527", "fceca579efcef09eb507c6ca977ea281")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("5659292833ec421da11ebde005d9c9a8", "d30cc10d54ebc967c8538ff74f442eee", "18a7251ddde77ed24bc54700d84d9be1", "f280e12f51f996dae7fffc64a56ee527", "fceca579efcef09eb507c6ca977ea281") or SHA1 in~ ("5659292833ec421da11ebde005d9c9a8", "d30cc10d54ebc967c8538ff74f442eee", "18a7251ddde77ed24bc54700d84d9be1", "f280e12f51f996dae7fffc64a56ee527", "fceca579efcef09eb507c6ca977ea281") or MD5 in~ ("5659292833ec421da11ebde005d9c9a8", "d30cc10d54ebc967c8538ff74f442eee", "18a7251ddde77ed24bc54700d84d9be1", "f280e12f51f996dae7fffc64a56ee527", "fceca579efcef09eb507c6ca977ea281")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["5659292833ec421da11ebde005d9c9a8", "d30cc10d54ebc967c8538ff74f442eee", "18a7251ddde77ed24bc54700d84d9be1", "f280e12f51f996dae7fffc64a56ee527", "fceca579efcef09eb507c6ca977ea281"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] C2 callback to Laravel Lang stealer infrastructure (flipboxstudio.info) Command & Control High
Detects any DNS resolution or outbound HTTP(S) connection to flipboxstudio.info, the attacker-controlled C2 used by the hijacked Laravel Lang Composer packages to pull the second-stage PHP credential stealer and exfiltrate harvested secrets. Any hit on a developer workstation or CI runner is high-fidelity confirmed compromise. Rationale: flipboxstudio.info is the only network IOC in the article and is named both as the dropper-pull host and the encrypted-exfil sink. A single hit equals confirmed install of the trojanised laravel-lang package on that host — the only reason a corporate endpoint resolves this domain.

[LLM] PHP / Composer spawns executable from %TEMP% (DebugElevator dropper) Installation High
Detects php.exe or php-cgi.exe spawning a *.exe child located under %TEMP% — the exact behaviour of the Laravel Lang stealer's PHP stage, which base64-decodes the embedded DebugElevator Windows binary, writes it to %TEMP% under a random filename, and launches it to crack Chromium App-Bound Encryption. Rationale: Article explicitly states: "the PHP payload also extracts a base64-encoded executable, which is written to the %TEMP% folder as a random .exe filename, and then launched." php.exe legitimately almost never spawns .exe children from %TEMP% — combination is article-specific and high-fidelity.

[LLM] Malicious helpers.php dropped under vendor/laravel-lang/ during Composer install Delivery High
Detects creation of a file named helpers.php under any vendor/laravel-lang/* directory — the exact indicator of the hijacked Laravel Lang packages (lang, http-statuses, attributes, actions). The legitimate packages do not ship a helpers.php under those directories; the malicious one is auto-registered in composer.json's autoload section and acts as the stage-1 dropper. Rationale: Article: "the malicious releases introduced a malicious file named 'src/helpers.php', which was automatically loaded by Composer." The combination of the exact filename + the exact namespace directory (vendor/laravel-lang/) is unique to the four hijacked packages; legitimate Laravel Lang releases prior to compromise did not ship this file. Lookback 60d covers the ~700 historical versions reportedly retagged.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1505.001 T1059.004

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize,

[LLM] Composer command line installing or updating laravel-lang/* packages (scope hunt) Delivery Medium
Hunting query to enumerate every host (dev workstation, CI runner, build agent, container image build) that explicitly invoked Composer to install/update/require any laravel-lang/* package during the compromise window. Used to scope the blast radius of which projects pulled the hijacked tags — pair with UC3 to confirm a malicious helpers.php landed. Rationale: Article names four affected packages (laravel-lang/lang, laravel-lang/http-statuses, laravel-lang/attributes, laravel-lang/actions) and notes ~700 historical versions retagged. The substring 'laravel-lang' on a Composer command line uniquely identifies install/update/require operations targeting any of them. Hunt-tier because composer require/update activity is legitimate on dev hosts — the value is enumeration, not alerting.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1199
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where (FileName =~ "composer" or FileName =~ "composer.phar" or FileName =~ "composer.bat"
         or ProcessCommandLine has "composer.phar"
         or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "php.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "composer"))
| where ProcessCommandLine has "laravel-lang"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Hits = count(),
            Cmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 25)
            by DeviceName, AccountName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where (TargetProcessName endswith "composer" or TargetProcessName endswith "composer.phar"

| order by LastSeen desc

[LLM] Chromium Local State / Login Data accessed by non-browser binary from %TEMP% (App-Bound Encryption theft) Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for a non-browser process — particularly one running from %TEMP% — touching Chrome/Brave/Edge 'Local State' or 'Login Data' files. This is the credential-access behaviour of the DebugElevator binary the Laravel Lang stealer drops on Windows, which extracts App-Bound Encryption keys to decrypt stored browser passwords. Rationale: Article: DebugElevator is "designed to target Chrome, Brave, and Edge, and extract App-Bound Encryption keys needed to decrypt stored browser credentials." The App-Bound Encryption master key lives in the Local State JSON and the encrypted passwords in Login Data — any non-browser binary touching those files, especially one running from %TEMP% under a php.exe parent, is the exact behaviour the article describes. Sigma + Datadog left empty because the detection depends on file-read telemetry that Sigma's file_event category and Sysmon EID 11 (FileCreate) do not natively capture; Falcon FileOpenInfo and Defender DeviceFileEvents (FileCopied/FileRenamed when stealer stages copies) do.

                                  @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data\",

| where (FileName in~ ("Local State", "Login Data", "Login Data.tmp", "Cookies", "Web Data"))
     or (PreviousFileName in~ ("Local State", "Login Data", "Cookies", "Web Data"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "brave.exe",

| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\",

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |

    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised Packagist Composer package vendor/ presence on hosts
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Packagist supply chain: Composer/npm postinstall fetching parikhpreyash4 GitHub payload · [LLM] Linux dotfile drop at /tmp/.sshd masquerading as OpenSSH daemon · [LLM] Build tooling spawning curl/wget with TLS verification disabled · Article-specific behavioural hunt — npm Adds 2FA-Gated Publishing and Package Install Controls Against Supply Chain
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] gvfsd-network binary executing from non-standard path (GNOME daemon masquerade)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] Packagist supply chain: Composer/npm postinstall fetching parikhpreyash4 GitHub payload Installation High
Detects the article-specific postinstall execution chain where Composer/npm build tooling spawns curl/wget/sh to retrieve the malicious Linux binary from github.com/parikhpreyash4/systemd-network-helper-aa5c751f or stages it to /tmp/.sshd. Targets developer endpoints and CI runners. Rationale: Uses three article-unique strings together — the attacker GitHub handle 'parikhpreyash4', the release asset name 'systemd-network-helper-aa5c751f', and the drop path '/tmp/.sshd'. Any one alone has effectively zero legitimate ground-truth, so cmd-line containment is a clean alerting signal.
ATT&CKT1546.016 T1204.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("parikhpreyash4", "systemd-network-helper-aa5c751f", "/tmp/.sshd")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("parikhpreyash4", "systemd-network-helper-aa5c751f", "/tmp/.sshd")
| extend BuildParent = iff(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","npx","yarn","pnpm","composer","composer.phar","php","sh","bash","dash","zsh"), true, false)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, BuildParent
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("parikhpreyash4", "systemd-network-helper-aa5c751f", "/tmp/.sshd")
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("parikhpreyash4", "systemd-network-helper-aa5c751f", "/tmp/.sshd")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Linux dotfile drop at /tmp/.sshd masquerading as OpenSSH daemon Installation High
Detects file creation at the exact /tmp/.sshd path used by the Packagist supply-chain postinstall stager. The dotfile prefix hides the artifact from default `ls`, and the .sshd name impersonates the OpenSSH daemon to blend into Linux process listings. Rationale: Exact path '/tmp/.sshd' is named verbatim in the Socket write-up as the stager's drop location. The dotfile-named-after-sshd pattern is so specific that any hit is high-fidelity; no legitimate Linux package or daemon writes to that exact path.
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath has "/tmp" and FileName == ".sshd")
   or FolderPath has "/tmp/.sshd"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath =~ "/tmp/.sshd"
   or (TargetFileName == ".sshd" and TargetFilePath has "/tmp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] gvfsd-network binary executing from non-standard path (GNOME daemon masquerade) Command & Control High
The campaign's second-stage binary is named 'gvfsd-network' to impersonate the legitimate GNOME Virtual File System daemon, which only lives in /usr/libexec or /usr/lib/gvfs. Anything by that name running from /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, or user home dirs is the implant. Rationale: Article cites 'The choice of the name "gvfsd-network" for the malware is interesting, as it refers to a GNOME Virtual File System (GVfs) daemon'. The legit binary's install path is fixed by distro packaging, so an allow-list of /usr/libexec + /usr/lib/gvfs is exhaustive — anything else with that name is the implant.
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "gvfsd-network"
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/usr/libexec" or FolderPath startswith "/usr/lib/gvfs" or FolderPath startswith "/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/gvfs")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "/gvfsd-network" or TargetProcessName =~ "gvfsd-network"
| where not (TargetProcessName startswith "/usr/libexec/" or TargetProcessName startswith "/usr/lib/gvfs/" or TargetProcessName startswith "/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/gvfs/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Build tooling spawning curl/wget with TLS verification disabled Installation Medium
The Socket write-up flags TLS-verification bypass as a hide-activity tactic of the malicious postinstall script. Detects curl/wget invocations with --insecure/-k/--no-check-certificate when the parent is a JS/PHP package manager or shell launched by one, which is the article's specific install-time payload chain. Rationale: Article calls out 'disabling TLS verification' as a hide-activity tactic of the postinstall stager. Combining curl/wget + insecure flag + a package-manager parent is article-specific — legit npm/composer post-install scripts pulling assets over HTTPS without verification is itself a red flag worth alerting on.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--insecure", " -k ", "--no-check-certificate")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","npx","yarn","pnpm","composer","composer.phar","php","sh","bash","dash","zsh")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "/curl" or TargetProcessName endswith "/wget"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--insecure", " -k ", "--no-check-certificate")
| where ActingProcessName endswith_cs "node" or ActingProcessName endswith_cs "npm" or ActingProcessName endswith_cs "yarn" or ActingProcessName endswith_cs "pnpm" or ActingProcessName endswith_cs "composer" or ActingProcessName endswith_cs "composer.phar" or ActingProcessName endswith_cs "php" or ActingProcessName endswith_cs "sh" or ActingProcessName endswith_cs "bash"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Compromised Packagist Composer package vendor/ presence on hosts Delivery High
Hunting query that surfaces hosts (developer endpoints, CI runners) where any of the 8 trojanized Composer packages was installed under vendor/. Composer drops package files at vendor/<vendor>/<package>/, so a file write to those exact paths is a strong inventory signal regardless of whether the postinstall fired. Rationale: Eight package names are listed verbatim in the article. Composer's deterministic vendor/<owner>/<name>/ install layout means a file write to one of those paths is direct evidence of installation, even if the postinstall script was blocked or already removed by the time of triage.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
let CompromisedPaths = dynamic([
    "/vendor/moritz-sauer-13/silverstripe-cms-theme/",
    "/vendor/crosiersource/crosierlib-base/",
    "/vendor/devdojo/wave/",
    "/vendor/devdojo/genesis/",
    "/vendor/katanaui/katana/",
    "/vendor/elitedevsquad/sidecar-laravel/",
    "/vendor/r2luna/brain/",
    "/vendor/baskarcm/tzi-chat-ui/"
]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where FolderPath has_any (CompromisedPaths)
| where FileName in~ ("package.json","composer.json","composer.lock")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), WriteCount = count(), AnyInitiator = any(InitiatingProcessFileName), AnyCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
          by DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName
| order by FirstSeen desc

ImFileEvent

| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), WriteCount = count(), AnyActor = any(ActorUsername), AnyProcess = any(ActingProcessName)
          by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

ATT&CKT1486

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Laravel-Lang supply chain C2/exfil to flipboxstudio.info Command & Control High
Hunts DNS lookups, SNI, or HTTP host headers to flipboxstudio[.]info — the C2/exfil domain used by the May 2026 Laravel-Lang Composer package compromise. The domain hosts both /payload (second-stage) and /exfil (stolen secrets), so any traffic to it from a Laravel-running host or CI runner indicates active compromise. Rationale: flipboxstudio[.]info is the single attacker-controlled C2/exfil endpoint named in the Snyk advisory and corroborated by StepSecurity, The Hacker News, Socket and Cyberpress. The domain has no legitimate use, so any successful resolution or connection is high-fidelity. Hits both DNS and HTTP/SNI telemetry to catch the resolution even if the payload connection is blocked. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/laravel-lang-supply-chain-attack • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/laravel-lang-php-packages-compromised.html • https://socket.dev/blog/laravel-lang-compromise • https://github.com/Laravel-Lang/http-statuses/issues/277
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1195.002

[LLM] Laravel-Lang stealer file drop in .laravel_locale temp directory Installation High
Hunts file creation under any .laravel_locale subdirectory of a temp path. The Snyk advisory documents three artifacts under <tmp>/.laravel_locale/: an md5-hashed infection marker, a 12-hex-char .php second-stage stealer, and (on Windows) an 8-hex-char .vbs launcher. The directory name is unique to this campaign and has no benign use. Rationale: The Snyk IOC table explicitly names <tmp>/.laravel_locale/<md5>, <tmp>/.laravel_locale/<12 hex>.php, and <tmp>/.laravel_locale/<8 hex>.vbs as stealer artifacts; StepSecurity corroborates the /tmp staging behaviour. The directory string is unique to this campaign and matches regardless of whether tmp resolves to /tmp, $TMPDIR, or %TEMP%. The filename regex extensions tag which stage fired for fast triage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/laravel-lang-supply-chain-attack • https://socket.dev/blog/laravel-lang-compromise
ATT&CKT1059 T1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has ".laravel_locale"
| extend Marker = iff(FileName matches regex @"^[a-f0-9]{32}$", "infection_marker", "")
| extend Stage2 = iff(FileName matches regex @"^[a-f0-9]{12}\.php$", "stealer_php", "")
| extend VbsLauncher = iff(FileName matches regex @"^[a-f0-9]{8}\.vbs$", "vbs_launcher", "")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, Marker, Stage2, VbsLauncher, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has ".laravel_locale"
| extend Marker = iff(TargetFileName matches regex @"^[a-f0-9]{32}$", "infection_marker", "")
| extend Stage2 = iff(TargetFileName matches regex @"^[a-f0-9]{12}\.php$", "stealer_php", "")
| extend VbsLauncher = iff(TargetFileName matches regex @"^[a-f0-9]{8}\.vbs$", "vbs_launcher", "")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, Marker, Stage2, VbsLauncher
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] DebugChromium.exe execution (Laravel-Lang stealer Windows artifact) Installation High
Hunts execution of DebugChromium.exe anywhere on disk. The Snyk advisory names this binary as a Windows artifact observed on hosts infected by the Laravel-Lang Composer supply-chain stealer. The name impersonates a Chrome debug build to blend in with developer tooling; there is no legitimate Microsoft/Google binary by this name. Rationale: DebugChromium.exe is called out by name in the Snyk IOC table as a Windows artifact observed on infected hosts. The string is unique - no legitimate Microsoft or Google product ships a binary by this name - so a process-create on this filename is essentially confirmation of infection. Captures parent (likely cscript.exe from UC4) for chain reconstruction. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/laravel-lang-supply-chain-advisory/ • https://securityonline.info/laravel-lang-supply-chain-attack-rce-backdoor/
